The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-4.$ Hence, $c=-4.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,-2),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=-2$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}-4 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}-4 & =-2 \\ k-4 & =-2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=2-(-4)=6.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}-4.$
